sections.h2: Can someone become the owner of a New Mexico house just by living in it?
sections.html:
Only if they meet every element of the adverse possession statute for ten years, and that includes holding some written document that looks like a title and paying the property taxes. Section 37-1-22 NMSA 1978 is the controlling law. A person who occupies a vacant house without any paper claim, and without paying the tax bill, does not come close.

The statute asks for adverse possession "continuously and in good faith under color of title for ten years," with no lawsuit brought by the true owner in that time. When those conditions are met, the occupant may keep the land described in the writing that gives color of title, and an owner who sat on a claim for the ten years is barred. The statute defines adverse possession as "an actual and visible appropriation of land, commenced and continued under a color of title and claim of right inconsistent with and hostile to the claim of another."

The statute ends with a separate tax condition. Adverse possession is not established unless the party claiming it, or those the party claims through, continuously paid all state, county and municipal taxes assessed against the property during the ten years.

sections.h2: What are the elements a claimant has to prove?
sections.html:
The New Mexico Attorney General's guide on adverse possession, prepared by New Mexico Legal Aid for the Land Grant Council, sums them up as three groups. The claimant needs open, continuous, exclusive, actual, visible, hostile and notorious possession for ten years, color of title, and payment of taxes. The guide says all of them must be met for the full ten years, and that failing any one defeats the claim.

  • Continuous: possession cannot be intermittent.
  • Actual: the claimant must physically enter. The guide says holding a deed is not enough, because the ten years do not begin until the claimant enters and takes possession.
  • Open and notorious: the claimant cannot hide. The clock does not run until the possession is visible enough to give the owner notice.
  • Exclusive: possession cannot be shared with the public or other users. If others try to use the land, the claimant has to keep them out.
  • Hostile: the occupant must be there without any right or permission, so that the possession is plainly against the owner's rights.

The annotations add that the claimant carries the burden. A party must prove adverse possession by clear and convincing evidence, and it cannot be established by inference or implication.

sections.h2: What is color of title, and what counts?
sections.html:
Color of title is a written document that purports to give the occupant title, even if it turns out to be defective. The Attorney General guide lists documents New Mexico courts have accepted: quitclaim deeds, a certificate of sale for taxes, a government patent, a void deed, and a quiet title decree or other court judgment.

The annotations to 37-1-22 give more detail. A recorded quitclaim deed, executed and acknowledged one day and recorded the next, with the buyer taking immediate possession, established color of title in one case. A tax deed can serve even when void for lack of title in the grantor, but not if its land description is too weak to identify the property. In one case involving siblings who owned together, a deed to one sibling and his wife did not establish color of title.

For owners, the lesson is that a stray deed in the record can matter. If someone is living in your house and has recorded a deed, even a weak one, the ten-year clock may have started. Our New Mexico quitclaim deed guide explains the form that often shows up in these disputes.

sections.h2: Does a tenant or a guest ever become an adverse possessor?
sections.html:
Almost never, because permission defeats hostility. The annotations say that where the original entry was permissive, the statute of limitations does not begin to run until an adverse holding is declared and notice of the change reaches the owner. Mere possession is not enough. Possession that starts as a tenancy is presumed permissive, and ending that presumption takes proof or a presumption of notice to the owner that the occupant now claims against them.

A person who enters a vacant house without permission is in a different position, but the extra requirements still apply. The Attorney General guide describes cases where claimants won by marking boundaries, posting no-trespassing signs, clearing land, fencing, limiting access and paying taxes. Those facts, taken together, gave the owner notice. Simply staying in a house, with none of those steps, is thin evidence.

The statute also protects some owners with a disability. If the person entitled to sue was imprisoned, of unsound mind or under the age of majority when the cause of action first accrued, they get one year after the disability ends to bring suit. The statute says cumulative disabilities do not extend the bar.

sections.h2: What about government land, water rights and land grants?
sections.html:
The statute does not reach every kind of property. The Attorney General guide says adverse possession usually cannot be applied against governmental property, only private property. It also explains that land grants governed as political subdivisions were made immune from adverse possession claims in 2007 under 49-1-11.2, except for claims that had already vested by June 15, 2007.

The annotations add two more limits. New Mexico's water code means water rights cannot be obtained through adverse possession, and the state's rights in highways cannot be divested by it under a cross-referenced statute.

sections.h2: How does an owner remove someone who has no right to be there?
sections.html:
Through a court case. The New Mexico Courts self-help guide says a landlord must go to court before evicting a tenant, and that a person living in a home who is not on the lease cannot be evicted like a tenant. That person is removed through "forcible entry," using Form 4-203, Complaint in Forcible Entry. At the hearing, the judge decides whether the person must leave and how much time they have to move out.

Section 35-10-1 NMSA 1978 lists the grounds for a forcible entry or unlawful detainer action in magistrate court. The first applies directly to uninvited occupants: the defendant entered and occupied the land of another against the owner's will or consent and refused to vacate after notice from the owner, agent or attorney. The other grounds cover:

  • A tenant who holds over after the lease ends or contrary to its terms.
  • A tenant who fails to pay rent when due.
  • An occupant who stays after a mortgage foreclosure or execution sale, unless claiming title paramount to the mortgage or derived from the purchaser.
  • A month-to-month tenant or tenant at will who stays after thirty days' written notice to vacate.

The district court has concurrent jurisdiction when the rent or reasonable rental value is $50 or more per month. An annotation also notes that these actions are summary proceedings that settle nothing about title. A forcible entry case puts the parties back in their prior positions but does not decide who owns the house.

sections.h2: When is trespassing a crime in New Mexico?
sections.html:
Section 30-14-1.1 NMSA 1978 makes several kinds of trespass a misdemeanor. A person who enters and remains on the lands of another after having been requested to leave commits one. So does a person who enters land posted against trespass at every roadway or apparent way of access, and a person who drives a vehicle onto fenced land except through an apparent way of access.

The same section creates civil liability. A person who enters another's land without permission and damages the realty or its improvements, including buildings, structures, trees and shrubs, owes double the appraised value of the damage to the owner, lessee or person in lawful possession.

The offense turns on a request to leave, so a dated written request is worth keeping. Talk to an attorney before acting.

sections.h2: What should an owner do to protect a vacant or inherited house?
sections.html:
Keep the paper record clean and the taxes current. Several steps follow from the statute and the guides:

  • Visit the property on a schedule, and document each visit with dates and photos.
  • Post no-trespassing signs and keep the property secured.
  • Pay the property tax yourself. The tax condition in the statute means a claimant who has not paid cannot succeed, and a delinquency can lead to a tax sale, covered in our New Mexico tax deed guide.
  • Check the county clerk's records for any deed or affidavit recorded by someone else.
  • Give written notice to anyone staying without permission, and keep a copy.

An annotation to the Property Tax Code, citing a 1954 decision, says the general rule is that continuity of adverse possession is interrupted if the land is forfeited to the state for taxes. That is one more reason to keep the tax record current.

Owners who inherited a house and cannot manage an occupant, repairs or back taxes sometimes sell as-is. Cash Home Buyers does not promise a price in advance. Anyone who buys will want to know who lives in the house and whether a court case is pending, so share that up front.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in New Mexico?
faqs.a: Ten years of continuous possession under color of title, in good faith, with all taxes paid, under 37-1-22 NMSA 1978. The claimant must prove it by clear and convincing evidence.

faqs.q: Do squatters have rights in New Mexico?
faqs.a: A person without a written claim to title and without paying the property taxes cannot meet the statute. The owner removes an occupant through a forcible entry complaint in court.

faqs.q: Do adverse possession claimants have to pay property taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The statute says adverse possession is not established unless the claimant or predecessors continuously paid all state, county and municipal taxes assessed during the ten years.

faqs.q: How do I remove someone who is not on the lease?
faqs.a: The New Mexico Courts self-help guide says to file Form 4-203, Complaint in Forcible Entry. The judge decides whether the person must leave and sets the time to move out.

faqs.q: Is it a crime to stay on someone's land after being told to leave?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 30-14-1.1 makes it a misdemeanor to enter and remain on the lands of another after having been requested to leave.

faqs.q: Can someone claim a New Mexico house after an eviction-type dispute?
faqs.a: A forcible entry or unlawful detainer case does not decide title, according to the annotations to 35-10-1. A separate action would be needed to settle ownership.
